term.name: Initialization vector (IV)
term.short: An initialization vector is a non-secret input that initializes a cipher mode so repeated plaintext does not produce unsafe repeated ciphertext.
term.meta_description: Learn what an IV does, how requirements differ between CBC, CTR, and other modes, and why an IV is not a key or universally interchangeable with a nonce.

body.title: Definition
body.html: An initialization vector is an additional input that sets the starting state of a cipher mode. It allows the same plaintext encrypted under the same key to produce different ciphertext and prevents patterns from repeating across messages.

body.title: Requirements depend on the mode
body.html: An IV is usually transmitted with the ciphertext and need not be secret. CBC requires an unpredictable fresh IV, while CTR-like modes primarily require a unique counter or nonce. Using the wrong generation rule can compromise security.

body.title: IV versus nonce
body.html: The terms overlap but are not universal synonyms. A nonce emphasizes non-repetition; IV is the initialization input defined by a mode. Some APIs call the same field an IV even when its essential requirement is uniqueness rather than randomness.

faq.question: Can the IV be stored with the ciphertext?
faq.answer: Yes, and this is normal. Security depends on satisfying the mode’s uniqueness or unpredictability rule, not on hiding the IV.

faq.question: Can one IV be reused with the same key?
faq.answer: Usually no. The exact damage varies by mode, from revealing equality to exposing plaintext or enabling forgery.

faq.question: Is an IV derived from a password?
faq.answer: It should be generated according to the mode, independently of password-derived key material unless a reviewed protocol specifies otherwise.
